poems.title: Out of Life
poems.logline: A poet reads aloud to a lover's turned back; the vape haze claims the room, the lover falls off the fire escape, and the poet falls behind — out of life — until it gets as dark as black.
poems.thesis: The way out he searches for (hallways, drawers, fire escapes) is the way down; leaving is not an exit but a direction.
poems.tagline: the maze, the haze, the fall, the ember

poems.seed:
STYLE. Afrofuturist Atlantis: a Black harbour city that kept its flood. Old walls carry a salt line at four metres. Ruins are mended in white ceramic seamed with light. Rusted teal steel, painted plywood, wet asphalt as a mirror. Photographic, practical light sources, humid air. The future here is repaired and inherited, never chrome or sterile.
EYE. 37mm equivalent, camera 1.1 m off the ground, eye-level, measured across 19 of this poem's shots. Static wide of the bare room, poet in the foreground, window and ex's back deep in frame; insert on the tv.
LIGHT. Evening into night; the fire escape at dusk. Dense orange fog at every hour; the sun is a disc or nothing. Low-pressure sodium (the new boroughs): a single orange wavelength that greys every other colour. Deep brown skin lit with full tonal range: a warm key and a rim light in the district's glow colour. Never crushed to a flat silhouette unless the beat asks for one.
PLACE. Dim bedroom; Poet reads to an averted Ex. Ex on the fire escape. Television showing world chaos. POET reads the poem aloud to the EX; the TV shows the world's chaos. The severn, a high bedroom; the hive's needles fill the window.
PEOPLE. Everyone here is Black. The Poet (Black man, thirties; matte black fitted mock-neck long sleeve, black trousers, black boots; a thin seam of white light from collar to heart that brightens when he speaks); close-cropped hair, short beard; unhurried, hands open. The Ex (Black man, thirties; long sodium-orange coat with teal lining over a charcoal knit, dark jeans, white trainers; a vape whose ember pulses cyan-white); leaner and taller than the Poet, locs gathered at the nape; seen from behind or in profile unless a beat says he turns. The Crowd (Black men and women, every age; club and street clothes in teal, orange and white: vests, wide trousers, head wraps, sneakers); moving together. The Poet and the Ex were lovers: two Black gay men. Their intimacy is shown by distance closing or opening, by hands, by foreheads, by who turns away. Tender and adult, never a spectacle, never a joke.
WATER. His words become vapour. When he speaks, vapour rises from where he stands; when he is silent it stills and mirrors the light. It runs thin and quick as rain. It starts along the floor and ends filling the room. It never puts out a light and never hides a face.
SOUND. Engines ticking under the decks, a far train, your own steps on concrete. Under it, room for one man's speaking voice.
MOOD. Disillusionment, Emptiness, Yearning, Loss, Anxiety, Desire for freedom. Close, dim and withholding; yearning becomes spatial distance.

poems.title: Flashing Lights
poems.logline: Floating in black between caving walls, a poet's eyes dilate until the pupil swallows the frame — and inside is age six: a window, a winding road, arguing headlights, a ghost with a tambourine, and the first throw.
poems.thesis: The silent scream and the silent call are the same instrument; the tambourine is the first time the poet answers noise with noise.

poems.title: How to Break off an Engagement
poems.logline: The tambourine thrown at age six flies into a chapel still whole, waits at the altar step through the cobwebs, and a time-lapse storm takes the building down to two stubs and a doorway — then the storm ends, the film turns white, and the tambourine falls one last time and shatters among two sets of footprints.
poems.thesis: An engagement is broken the way a chapel decays: first the cross tilts, then the roof, then the register of the world itself — and the gift that started it all only breaks after everything it was thrown at is gone.
poems.tagline: the storm takes everything that was ever called goods

poems.title: Nevermore
poems.logline: In red and black, hands in pockets, a poet walks the shore of everything that broke, lets a heart lift itself back into his chest, follows the trail into a night that falls through the film's own register, and searches a bare field until his hands — they too used to be his — return, and the arms are drawn for the first time.

STYLE. Afrofuturist Atlantis: a Black harbour city that kept its flood. Old walls carry a salt line at four metres. Ruins are mended in white ceramic seamed with light. None of its own: dawn and dusk; a few lanterns on the steps; one sodium platform lamp left from the new boroughs. Deep brown skin lit with full tonal range: a warm key and a rim light in the district's glow colour. Never crushed to a flat silhouette unless the beat asks for one.

The Poet (Black man, thirties; matte black fitted mock-neck long sleeve, black trousers, black boots; a thin seam of white light from collar to heart that brightens when he speaks); close-cropped hair, short beard; unhurried, hands open. poems.logline: Down a road that lights its own bricks, past comets all pointing one way, the poet watches a drowned city let go of its water, pays the gate with one of his named stars, wanders streets where every joyful noise blooms a rainbow, stands in a plaza until the whole city blinks with his heart — and follows the music into a house.
poems.thesis: A city born in unison out of the purest of fictions is entered the way faith is: you pay with something you were just given a name for, and the light at the door costs you your own.
poems.tagline: a city comes up out of the water
poems.eye: 26mm equivalent, camera 1.2 m off the ground, eye-level, measured across 25 of this poem's shots
poems.seed:
STYLE. Afrofuturist Atlantis: a Black harbour city that kept its flood. Old walls carry a salt line at four metres. Ruins are mended in white ceramic seamed with light. Rusted teal steel, painted plywood, wet asphalt as a mirror. Photographic, practical light sources, humid air. The future here is repaired and inherited, never chrome or sterile.
EYE. 26mm equivalent, camera 1.2 m off the ground, eye-level, measured across 25 of this poem's shots. Low wide on the gates opening, poet entering frame from behind camera; reverse to the city glowing through.
LIGHT. Still night; warm-lit windows. Clear. The gate's white ceramic lit from inside; fences of light at the perimeter (cyan, high-frequency). Deep brown skin lit with full tonal range: a warm key and a rim light in the district's glow colour. Never crushed to a flat silhouette unless the beat asks for one.
PLACE. Winged marble gates open. Marble gates with wings swing open to an ancestral orchestra; a line of figures, the POET among them, walks through into the radiant city. The light gate, from the field.
PEOPLE. Everyone here is Black. The Poet (Black man, thirties; matte black fitted mock-neck long sleeve, black trousers, black boots; a thin seam of white light from collar to heart that brightens when he speaks); close-cropped hair, short beard; unhurried, hands open. The Child (Black boy, about eight; yellow raincoat over striped pyjamas, bare feet); short curls; the Poet as a child. The Ancestors (Black women and men, every age; white ceramic-plate collars over long indigo and ochre robes, cowrie and brass at the wrists, bare feet); walking in procession, faces calm. The Elders (Black women and men, seventies and older; layered white linen, wide-brimmed hats, carved canes, gold rings); seated or standing still. The Crowd (Black men and women, every age; club and street clothes in teal, orange and white: vests, wide trousers, head wraps, sneakers); moving together. The Figures (Black men and women, every age; long coats and wraps in rusted teal and white); seen at a distance.
WATER. His words become liquid light. When he speaks, liquid light rises from where he stands; when he is silent it stills and mirrors the light. It runs slow as oil. It starts a thread on the ground and ends a full bright flood. It never puts out a light and never hides a face.
SOUND. The ancestral orchestra; the heart-scan's tone; ten thousand people breathing. Under it, room for one man's speaking voice.
MOOD. Awe, Hope, Unity, Peace, Serenity, Collective evolution. Expansive, serene and welcoming; belonging is expressed through shared rhythms.

poems.title: DJ Turn Me Up
poems.logline: A DJ is lowered into the house on a beam of light, the needle rings the room, and the poet — eyes wide shut, chin nested down — tells the whole love story over a rising fader: ghosts in vineyards, rings diverging, a home trucked apart, eleven petals plunked off a daisy, three roads and one silver lining — until the chin nests high and the volume clips.
poems.thesis: Being heard is a gain structure: the same story at level one is grief and at level eight is testimony — the fader, not the words, is what turns forth to face delights and shadows.

poems.title: Newly Single

poems.thesis: Separation is a frame-rate: the body grieves at the world's speed and the soul at its own — and what returns from the split is not relief but accuracy: what isn't mine, I still can not give.

poems.title: Yet Heard
poems.logline: Through a fawning crowd, past a moon that runs its phases over one walk, into a phone booth twice — mother's living room arriving as an inset with a tear down its crease, father's footprints lighting under his son's feet — while the break-up widens in the background of every shot, until the EX dissolves to weather and a motorcycle blinks its lamp at the man left standing.
poems.thesis: Farewell is not an event but a background process: it runs at its own rate behind every call, every walk, every prayer — and being heard does not stop it; it only means someone watched it happen with you.

poems.seed:
STYLE. Afrofuturist Atlantis: a Black harbour city that kept its flood. Old walls carry a salt line at four metres. Ruins are mended in white ceramic seamed with light. Rusted teal steel, painted plywood, wet asphalt as a mirror. Photographic, practical light sources, humid air. The future here is repaired and inherited, never chrome or sterile.
EYE. 31mm equivalent, camera 1.6 m off the ground, eye-level, measured across 21 of this poem's shots. Handheld follow through the crowd; ex kept back-to-camera, soft focus, reaching hand in foreground.
LIGHT. Late night, moon up, wet pavement. Rain; wet pavement mirrors everything. Led canopies and neon: red-blue, pink; the booth's white. Deep brown skin lit with full tonal range: a warm key and a rim light in the district's glow colour. Never crushed to a flat silhouette unless the beat asks for one.
PLACE. Rooftop gaze toward distant mountains. Leaving the club amid fawning crowds, the POET glimpses the EX from behind and reaches for him but cannot get through. The sidewalk at the foot of the spire.
PEOPLE. Everyone here is Black. The Poet (Black man, thirties; matte black fitted mock-neck long sleeve, black trousers, black boots; a thin seam of white light from collar to heart that brightens when he speaks); close-cropped hair, short beard; unhurried, hands open. The Ex (Black man, thirties; long sodium-orange coat with teal lining over a charcoal knit, dark jeans, white trainers; a vape whose ember pulses cyan-white); leaner and taller than the Poet, locs gathered at the nape; seen from behind or in profile unless a beat says he turns. The Mother (Black woman, sixties; indigo wrap dress, gold hoop earrings, cream cardigan, house slippers); silver-streaked hair pinned up. The Father (Black man, sixties; pressed white shirt with sleeves rolled, brown wool trousers, braces, reading glasses); grey beard, shaved head. The Crowd (Black men and women, every age; club and street clothes in teal, orange and white: vests, wide trousers, head wraps, sneakers); moving together. The Poet and the Ex were lovers: two Black gay men. Their intimacy is shown by distance closing or opening, by hands, by foreheads, by who turns away. Tender and adult, never a spectacle, never a joke.
WATER. His words become vapour. When he speaks, vapour rises from where he stands; when he is silent it stills and mirrors the light. It runs with the weight of water. It starts along the floor and ends filling the room. It never puts out a light and never hides a face.
SOUND. Neon hum, the booth's dial tone, a moped, the canopy's advertisements. Under it, room for one man's speaking voice.
MOOD. Unspoken longing, Enduring connection, Melancholy, Comfort, Seeking validation, Processing grief. Tender but unresolved; adjacent spaces hold grief without settling it.

poems.title: Magic Ride

poems.title: New Day
poems.logline: The fog exhales its introduction over the ruin, and the ruin answers by lifting itself: stones float into a new base course, the broken arch straightens into a doorway, a parabolic shell draws itself left to right — and when the water arrives edgeless, the temple learns to reflect, the poet walks the waterline with his own inversion underfoot, and the sun ends up overhead.
poems.thesis: Catharsis is construction with the original materials: nothing new arrives — the same stones, the same arch, the same man — only the schedule runs the other way.

STYLE. Afrofuturist Atlantis: a Black harbour city that kept its flood. Old walls carry a salt line at four metres. Ruins are mended in white ceramic seamed with light. Rusted teal steel, painted plywood, wet asphalt as a mirror. Photographic, practical light sources, humid air. The future here is repaired and inherited, never chrome or sterile.

PLACE. Return to chapel shore and dismount. The motorcycle comes down out of the hills to the chapel shore; wide view of distant seas and the wooded hills behind. The shore steps beneath the mountain.
PEOPLE. Everyone here is Black. The Poet (Black man, thirties; matte black fitted mock-neck long sleeve, black trousers, black boots; a thin seam of white light from collar to heart that brightens when he speaks); close-cropped hair, short beard; unhurried, hands open. poems.title: Reunion
poems.logline: Decades later, inside the temple they rebuilt, three friends arrive through a door of light, trade their words in for laughter, go quiet for the crowned elders who stand faintly among them, flip the burning hourglass rather than let the occasion be one-time — and part ways trailing curls of wind, hearts still blinking in unison.
poems.thesis: Brotherhood is a shared clock: the hug synchronizes it, the laughter funds it, the flip extends it — and the winds can part ways without breaking the tempo.
poems.tagline: less time for words, more space for laughter

poems.title: How to Win My Heart
poems.logline: At the harbor cafe he watches couples orbit like Jupiter's moons and elders clutch what they kept, while his own love stories sit char-eaten at his elbow — so he harvests the flowers into his power instead, until a distant lit window says YOU'LL SEE ME, and instead of leaving toward anything, he sets the bouquet on the rail and sits back down: don't make me leave; I escaped here for a reason.
poems.thesis: Winning this heart is not pursuit but placement: stay where you escaped to, put the gathered power somewhere visible, and let the window keep its light on.

The Poet (Black man, thirties; matte black fitted mock-neck long sleeve, black trousers, black boots; a thin seam of white light from collar to heart that brightens when he speaks); close-cropped hair, short beard; unhurried, hands open. The Ex (Black man, thirties; long sodium-orange coat with teal lining over a charcoal knit, dark jeans, white trainers; a vape whose ember pulses cyan-white); leaner and taller than the Poet, locs gathered at the nape; seen from behind or in profile unless a beat says he turns. The Child (Black boy, about eight; yellow raincoat over striped pyjamas, bare feet); short curls; the Poet as a child. The Crowd (Black men and women, every age; club and street clothes in teal, orange and white: vests, wide trousers, head wraps, sneakers); moving together. The Couple (Black two men, thirties; one in the Poet's matte black, one in the Ex's sodium-orange coat); close, foreheads nearly touching. The Figures (Black men and women, every age; long coats and wraps in rusted teal and white); seen at a distance. The Poet and the Ex were lovers: two Black gay men. Their intimacy is shown by distance closing or opening, by hands, by foreheads, by who turns away. Tender and adult, never a spectacle, never a joke.
WATER. His words become tide water. When he speaks, tide water rises from where he stands; when he is silent it stills and mirrors the light. It runs with the weight of water. It starts at the soles and ends chest-deep. It never puts out a light and never hides a face.
SOUND. The harbour slapping the piles, gulls, a café's cups, the sleep-dam pumping. Under it, room for one man's speaking voice.
MOOD. Solitude, Weariness, Vulnerability, Hope, Desire for recognition/connection, Overcoming past defeats. Watchful and guarded; attention gradually risks remaining with another person.

poems.title: Hot Minute
poems.logline: The haze gathers on the water and takes everything he built — boats, cafe, her window gently, the flowers last — then takes him ground-up until only the pulse blinks in the black. What follows is the suite remembering itself in twelve flashes, a dance of two entwined muses around one center, and an old vintage door opening on a slow warm party: the kind he once fell out of a window to escape, and now walks into, from the back, at his own speed, as the door closes and keeps him.
poems.thesis: Leaving and arriving are the same door seen from different registers: the suite opens with a fall out of a window and closes with a walk through a door — and the victory is not escaping the party, but choosing it.
poems.tagline: everything learns to be weather, then a door
poems.eye: 28mm equivalent, camera 1.3 m off the ground, eye-level, measured across 24 of this poem's shots
poems.seed:
STYLE. Afrofuturist Atlantis: a Black harbour city that kept its flood. Old walls carry a salt line at four metres. Ruins are mended in white ceramic seamed with light. Rusted teal steel, painted plywood, wet asphalt as a mirror. Photographic, practical light sources, humid air. The future here is repaired and inherited, never chrome or sterile.
EYE. 28mm equivalent, camera 1.3 m off the ground, eye-level, measured across 24 of this poem's shots. Slow tilt up the body as haze climbs; hand gripping a frame edge in close-up.
LIGHT. Timeless; the party reads as night. Dense orange fog at every hour; the sun is a disc or nothing. Low-pressure sodium (the new boroughs): a single orange wavelength that greys every other colour. Deep brown skin lit with full tonal range: a warm key and a rim light in the district's glow colour. Never crushed to a flat silhouette unless the beat asks for one.
PLACE. Harbor, temple, Atlantis dissolve into haze. Haze rises from the ground and covers him; he is reluctant at first, then gives in. The harbour edge, then the end of the catwalk.
PEOPLE. Everyone here is Black. The Poet (Black man, thirties; matte black fitted mock-neck long sleeve, black trousers, black boots; a thin seam of white light from collar to heart that brightens when he speaks); close-cropped hair, short beard; unhurried, hands open. The Friends (Black men and women, among them gay couples, twenties to forties; going-out clothes: mesh tops, silk shirts open at the collar, tailored shorts, bright sneakers, gold chains); laughing, arms around each other. The Crowd (Black men and women, every age; club and street clothes in teal, orange and white: vests, wide trousers, head wraps, sneakers); moving together. The Figures (Black men and women, every age; long coats and wraps in rusted teal and white); seen at a distance.
WATER. His words become vapour. When he speaks, vapour rises from where he stands; when he is silent it stills and mirrors the light. It runs with the weight of water. It starts along the floor and ends filling the room. It never puts out a light and never hides a face.
SOUND. Engines ticking under the decks, a far train, your own steps on concrete. Under it, room for one man's speaking voice.
MOOD. Intensity, Reluctance, Resignation, Acceptance, Resilience, Desire for permanence. Intense but accepting; built forms dissolve while remembered relations recur.
